slides.title: Chapter 8: Digital Signatures
slides.say: This deck explains how a Bitcoin signature works and what it commits to. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library. Bitcoin Core 31.1.0 was run once on a test network, and its answers are only read back.
slides.takeaway: What a signature proves and commits to, how Schnorr and ECDSA work, and what moved since print

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: The route has seven parts that follow the order of the chapter. Three true stories and twenty code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.takeaway: Seven parts, twenty examples, three true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.
slides.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

slides.title: One chapter, seven parts
slides.say: The chapter has seven parts and 45 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and some parts a true story. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
slides.takeaway: Seven parts; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures
slides.say: A digital signature is a proof that the holder of a private key approved a message. This part shows what verification needs, why two moduli appear, and what is really signed.
slides.takeaway: A signature is a wax seal that only the owner of the ring can press.

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures (1 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover Digital Signatures, How Digital Signatures Work and Creating a Digital Signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Three inputs, one answer
slides.say: Verification takes a message, a public key and a signature, and answers yes or no. We flip one bit of the message, then swap the key, and both attempts fail. Only the true triple passes. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Change the message, the key or the signature and the answer turns to False

slides.title: Foundations of digital signatures (2 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover Verifying the Signature and discrete logarithm problem. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Scalars wrap at n, coordinates at p
slides.say: The signature equation lives in the group of curve points, whose order is n. Reducing the response modulo n makes the equation hold, reducing it modulo p does not. The two numbers differ by 129 bits. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The book says everything is modulo p; the response is reduced modulo n

slides.title: What is signed is a digest
slides.say: A signature is made over a hash of selected transaction fields. The same transaction gives the same digest, and raising one output by a satoshi gives a completely different one, so the signature no longer fits. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The signature covers a hash of the transaction, not the bytes themselves

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH)
slides.say: A signature need not cover the whole transaction. One byte, the SIGHASH flag, chooses what it covers. We measure what each flag commits to and meet the bug of SINGLE.
slides.takeaway: A flag chooses how much of the letter the seal covers.

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (1 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover Signature Hash Types (SIGHASH), signature hash, SIGHASH_ALL and SIGHASH_NONE. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A flag is one byte
slides.say: The flag appended to a signature is a single byte. The three base flags are 1, 2 and 3. The modifier ANYONECANPAY is 128, the top bit, which is why it can be added to any base flag. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: ANYONECANPAY is the top bit, so it combines with every base flag

slides.title: Signature hash flags (SIGHASH) (2 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover SIGHASH_SINGLE, SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY, BIP118 and SIGHASH_DEFAULT. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: What each flag commits to
slides.say: We change one field of the transaction at a time and ask if the digest moves. ALL covers all five probed fields. The other flags leave some open, which is what lets others complete a transaction. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Only plain ALL covers every probed field, other inputs' sequences included

slides.title: SINGLE with no matching output
slides.say: SIGHASH_SINGLE signs the output with the same number as the input. For inputs one and two there is none, so the legacy algorithm signs the constant one, which holds for any transaction. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: A digest equal to the number one can be reused on any transaction

slides.title: Schnorr signatures
slides.say: Schnorr signatures began as a proof of identity. We turn the proof into a signature, meet the BIP340 format, and see why keys that add up bring both multisignatures and a trap.
slides.takeaway: Schnorr is a seal whose imprints can be added together.

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (1 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover Schnorr Signatures, Serialization of Schnorr Signatures, Schnorr-based Scriptless Multisignatures and Schnorr-based Scriptless Threshold Signatures. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The protocol with whole numbers
slides.say: The book teaches the protocol with whole numbers first. The proof works: s times G equals the commitment plus the challenge times the public key. But dividing the public key by G reveals the secret. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: With plain integers anyone divides and reads the secret; points forbid that

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (2 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover challenge, Fiat-Shamir transform, BIP340 and x-only public key. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: From identity proof to signature
slides.say: An honest prover's response passes and a wrong one fails. Letting a hash of the message choose the challenge turns the proof into a signature, and the signature fits only that message. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The hash of the message plays the examiner, so no examiner has to be online

slides.title: The signature that was patented for two decades
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 1991-02-19. Claus-Peter Schnorr published an efficient identification and signature scheme for smart cards in the proceedings of the Crypto '89 conference, and the United States published his patent 4,995,082 on 19 February 1991, filed on 23 February 1990 and claiming priority from 24 February 1989.
slides.takeaway: A patent decided which signature Bitcoin started with

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (3 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover linearity, batch verification, key prefixing and scriptless multisignature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A fixed size: 64 bytes
slides.say: A BIP340 public key is the x coordinate only, 32 bytes. The signature is 64 bytes, always. The ECDSA signature of the same key is written in DER, whose length varies by a byte or two. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Schnorr is smaller and of fixed size; DER signatures vary

slides.title: Schnorr signatures: key concepts (4 of 4)
slides.say: These cards cover key cancellation attack, MuSig2, Shamir secret sharing and scriptless threshold signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A key that cancels another key
slides.say: If keys are simply added, Bob can wait for Alice's key and publish a key that cancels it. Then Bob alone signs for both. With MuSig2's hashed weights the same attack no longer gives Bob's key. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: MuSig2 weights each key by a hash of all keys, which stops the trick

slides.title: Any two of three shares
slides.say: A secret is the height of a line at zero. Each of three shares is a point on that line. Any two points rebuild the line and give the secret, while one share alone fits every possible secret. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Fewer than the threshold reveal nothing; the threshold reveals everything

slides.title: ECDSA signatures
slides.say: ECDSA signed every Bitcoin payment from 2009 and still signs most. We run its formulas, take apart its byte layout and separate what miners enforce from what nodes prefer.
slides.takeaway: ECDSA is the older seal, with a messier imprint and two valid shapes.

slides.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover ECDSA Signatures, ECDSA Algorithm, Serialization of ECDSA Signatures (DER) and ECDSA. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: ECDSA with the book's formulas
slides.say: We sign with an explicit nonce and verify by rebuilding the point K. The second valid value of s is n minus s. Nodes relay only the smaller one, the low form. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: If s verifies, so does n minus s: the signature has two forms

slides.title: ECDSA signatures: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover R and s, malleability, DER and low-S rule. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Nine elements in 71 bytes
slides.say: DER writes the signature as nested fields: a type, a length, then R and s, each with its own tag and length, and a final hash-type byte. The byte counts add up to the signature. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Seven of the nine elements are one byte; R and s take 32 each

slides.title: The signature on the page is a real payment
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2013-12-27. The long hexadecimal string that chapter 8 of Mastering Bitcoin uses to explain the DER layout, beginning 3045022100884d142d, is not an invented example: it is the signature in the input of transaction 0627052b6f28912f2703066a912ea577f2ce4da4caa5a5fbd8a57286c345c2f2, mined in block 277,316 at 23:11:54 UTC on 27 December 2013.
slides.takeaway: The signature printed in the book is a real payment

slides.title: Valid for miners, refused by nodes
slides.say: Both forms of the signature verify, so a block that contains the high-S twin is valid. A node, however, relays only the low form. Policy is stricter than consensus, and can be changed without a fork. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Policy is a stricter house rule; consensus is the law

slides.title: Policy or consensus?
slides.say: High S is policy: miners accept it, nodes do not relay it. Strict DER became consensus in 2015. Keeping the two apart explains why a transaction can be valid and yet never reach a miner through ordinary nodes.
slides.takeaway: Policy can change with a release; consensus changes only by a fork

slides.title: Randomness and signature size
slides.say: A signature needs a number used once. If it repeats, the key leaks; if it is derived from key and message, it never repeats. The part ends with how it changes the signature size.
slides.takeaway: The nonce is a one-time pad: use it twice and the secret leaks.

slides.title: Randomness and signature size: key concepts
slides.say: These cards cover The Importance of Randomness in Signatures, nonce, RFC 6979 and nonce reuse. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: One nonce, two signatures, no secret
slides.say: Two signatures with the same nonce give two equations in two unknowns. Subtracting them reveals the nonce and then the private key. A different nonce for the second message leaves nothing to solve. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Android's weak generator made this attack possible in 2013

slides.title: When the phone's random numbers were not random
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2013-08-11. On 11 August 2013 Bitcoin.org published an alert that the Android component that generates secure random numbers contained critical weaknesses, which made every wallet generated on Android vulnerable to theft, and named Bitcoin Wallet, blockchain.info, BitcoinSpinner and Mycelium Wallet; Bitcoin Wallet 3.15 rotated keys automatically.
slides.takeaway: Weak randomness at signing time gives away the key

slides.title: The nonce derived from the key
slides.say: RFC 6979 derives the nonce by keyed hashing of the secret key and the message. It never repeats for different messages, and a signature can be repeated and compared exactly in a test. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Same key and message always give the same nonce, and so the same signature

slides.title: About half are one byte longer
slides.say: When the top bit of R is set, DER adds a zero byte, so the signature has 71 bytes instead of 70. Over 200 signatures about half are longer. Core grinds the nonce to avoid the extra byte. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Bitcoin Core signs again until R is small, to save a byte

slides.title: Segwit signing
slides.say: Segregated witness changed what is hashed when a transaction is signed. We count the bytes of the old and the new method and see why the amount is now part of the signature.
slides.takeaway: Segwit changed what is signed, as a cheque that also states the amount.

slides.title: Segwit signing: key concepts
slides.say: These cards cover Segregated Witness's New Signing Algorithm, BIP143, O(n) hashing and taproot signature. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 8.
slides.takeaway: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Quadratic hashing
slides.say: The old algorithm hashes almost the whole transaction again for every input. BIP143 hashes the shared parts once. The ratio of the two grows with the number of inputs. It is example 18 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: Doubling the inputs roughly quadruples the bytes the old method hashes

slides.title: BIP143 signs the amount
slides.say: In the old algorithm the signer never saw the value of the coin it spent. In BIP143 the amount is part of the digest, so a wrong amount gives a different digest and an invalid signature. It is example 19 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The new digest changes with the amount; the old one cannot

slides.title: Since the book went to print
slides.say: The book went to print in 2023 and the standards have moved. This part collects the dates, the status of the proposals and the evidence trail behind every number in the deck.
slides.takeaway: Standards move on after print, like a map that needs a new edition.

slides.title: Dates behind the patent and taproot
slides.say: United States law gave the longer of 17 years from grant or 20 years from filing. For Schnorr's patent that ends on 23 February 2010. Taproot activated 4,698 days after the genesis block. It is example 20 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.takeaway: The patent ended in 2010; taproot came eleven years later

slides.title: Status of the BIPs the chapter names
slides.say: The book states what was a draft in 2023. Counting the saved index of proposals shows six deployed, two complete, four drafts and one closed. A draft can still change, so check the index before you rely on a number.
slides.takeaway: A proposal's status can change after print; check the index

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.say: These five lines are the deck in miniature, one for each group of parts. A line that feels unproven should send you back to its code slide, because every figure in it was computed there. The chapter code tab of the course page reruns all twenty examples.
slides.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part carries the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Everything here is free to read or watch, and every link was opened on the date in the subtitle. A good start is the Optech workshop on Schnorr and taproot, then BIP340 read beside the chapter. The course page for chapter 8 carries the full text.
